name: Sweep from Chill Dog
summary: A sweep from Chill Dog needs a controlled posting arm and an off-balanced base; the high rubber-guard connection alone does not guarantee a reversal or mount.
description: A sweep from Chill Dog needs a controlled posting arm and an off-balanced base; the high rubber-guard connection alone does not guarantee a reversal or mount.
overview:
The bottom player faces the opponent in Chill Dog, with a high leg controlling posture. The reviewed rubber-guard instruction supports controlling posture and a posting arm. It does not establish this node's unspecified direct sweep to mount; a specific sweep setup must be chosen before live practice.

Keep the opposing hand on the mat and hug the knee before changing the head-side grip. Determine which arm can prevent the intended reversal; do not assume an isolated arm removes every post. Use a safe wrist or arm connection without manipulating individual fingers.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Brandon McCaghren — Gogoplata from rubber guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wn39-wrfsbs); [Eddie Bravo — Chill Dog / Invisible Collar clarification](https://www.10thplanetjj.com/forum/threads/17657-Chill-Dog-Invisible-Collar-Question).

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): What upper-body connection can help control one post?
flashcards.answer: Chill Dog can retain one arm outside through the New York wrap; that provides one control but not a complete sweep setup.
flashcards.answer_line: Overhook and knee hug trap that arm

plausible: Only a loose leg behind their head
Both hands pull head, arm stays free
trap: Knee high with the overhook open

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): What must you check before choosing a tipping direction?
flashcards.answer: One isolated arm does not remove every post. Assess the remaining supports before selecting a separately taught sweep.
flashcards.answer_line: Which hand or leg still bears weight

plausible: Only the arm already in the knee hug
Only knee width, ignoring free hand
trap: Low head, assuming no hand posts

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): Their free hand can stop the tip; how should your wrist grip work?
flashcards.answer: Use wrist or arm control to deny the hand a weight-bearing post in the chosen tipping direction. Mere wrist contact is insufficient if the palm can still reach the mat; do not substitute individual finger manipulation. This is a posting-control prerequisite for a separately established sweep, not a complete Chill Dog sweep sequence.
flashcards.answer_line: Stop that hand taking weight on mat

plausible: Hold wrist low, leave palm planted
Wrist contact, arm extends to post
trap: Let wrist go as hips start tipping

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): What should a small hip movement test?
flashcards.answer: A controlled balance check helps identify a usable opening without committing to an unsupported reversal.
flashcards.answer_line: Their base shifts; your guard stays

plausible: Head lowers, both knees stay planted
Knee hug tighter, their weight still
trap: Your hips move, their posts stay put

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): A chosen sweep stalls on their free hand; why?
flashcards.answer: The isolated arm is only one removed post. If the other hand supports their weight along the chosen sweep direction, the base remains.
flashcards.answer_line: Free hand bears weight along the tip

plausible: Knee hug already disables free hand
Low head prevents a loaded hand post
trap: Their leg base, with free hand idle

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): What must be checked after a separately established sweep?
flashcards.answer: Coming on top is not automatically mount; stabilize the position actually reached and clear legs as needed.
flashcards.answer_line: Actual pin and remaining leg traps

plausible: Only shoulder landing, ignore legs
Only freed legs, ignoring chest pin
trap: Only overhook retained, assume a pin

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): Their base stays stable as your high guard opens; what next?
flashcards.answer: If a sweep is unavailable and the high connection fails, retain guard with a frame and hip escape rather than forcing the reversal.

plausible: Pull head as both knees fall outside
Keep knee hug as proof of a sweep
trap: Keep tipping as shoulder fills gap

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (bottom): Which claim about one-arm control and the landing is accurate?
flashcards.answer: A posting-arm restriction is only part of a sweep; leg work, direction and the resulting top configuration still need establishment.
flashcards.answer_line: Other posts and landing still matter

plausible: Head height decides where you land
Overhook removes the other hand post
trap: Getting above hips clears both legs

It does not establish this node's unspecified direct sweep to mount; a specific sweep setup must be chosen before live practice.

Keep the free hand available for framing while preventing the isolated elbow from being pulled further away from your torso. The opponent changing the hand around your head signals the move beyond New York, not a turtle escape. Keep a safe base and prevent the free leg from closing high behind your head.

Recover the elbow toward your ribs only when the leg enclosure has slack, rather than jerking the shoulder. Bring the head and chest upright in stages after clearing the upper-body control. Do not drive the partner onto the neck or force the bent leg sideways to escape the control.

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (top): Which limb remains useful while the other arm is isolated?
flashcards.answer: Keep the available arm useful while avoiding further separation of the captured elbow; one trapped arm does not remove every support.
flashcards.answer_line: Free arm frames inside and balances

plausible: Trapped arm as a rigid extended post
Both hands reach for their ankle
trap: Free arm tucked behind your hip

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (top): What does the head-side grip change prove by itself?
flashcards.answer: A Chill Dog grip change concerns upper-body control; it does not establish that your base has been overturned.

plausible: Both your hand posts have gone
Your knees have lost mat support
trap: Your weight is beyond the leg base

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (top): What should you deny before their high clinch strengthens?
flashcards.answer: An early inside barrier can prevent the second leg reinforcing posture control while you preserve a balanced base.
flashcards.answer_line: Free leg closes behind your head

plausible: Free foot settles on the floor
Their knee returns below your chest
trap: Free foot on hip, below your ribs

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (top): What must happen before a large balance adjustment?
flashcards.answer: If the arm is fixed under the knee hug, release the shoulder connection before a large turn so it is not used as a lever.
flashcards.answer_line: Caught shoulder is free to move

plausible: Only free hand needs a mat post
Only feet need a wider stance

flashcards.question: Sweep from Chill Dog (top): When can you lift posture during the sweep threat?
flashcards.answer: Posture recovery follows release of the upper-body hold. Raising the chest against a fixed loop is not a reliable balance solution.

plausible: Whenever the free hand is on the mat
Whenever their hips move sideways
trap: Free leg moves; first shin tight
